defs: Distributed Denial-of-Service: many distributed systems overwhelm a target with traffic or requests.

course.learn: A Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack uses many systems or traffic sources to overwhelm a target's bandwidth, processing, connection tables, or application resources.
course.why: The distributed sources make blocking and attribution harder than a single-source DoS attack.
course.example: Thousands of compromised IoT devices send requests to an online store until legitimate customers cannot connect.
course.exam: Many sources + availability outage = DDoS. Layer-based attacks may target network/transport capacity or application resources.

course.learn: Security indicators are observable signs that may reveal compromise, misuse, or abnormal conditions. Examples include account lockouts, concurrent sessions, impossible travel, blocked content, missing logs, unusual resource consumption, and resources becoming inaccessible.
course.why: One indicator rarely proves an incident by itself. Analysts correlate multiple signals with normal baselines and context before deciding how to respond.
course.example: A user account signs in from two distant countries within minutes, generates repeated lockouts, and accesses resources at an unusual time. Together, the indicators justify investigation.
course.exam: CompTIA may present symptoms rather than name the attack. Identify what the indicator suggests, correlate evidence, and choose the next defensive action.

breakdown.explanation: This can be an observable clue during monitoring or investigation. It should be correlated with other evidence before concluding that an attack occurred.

defs: Domain Name System: translates names such as example.com into IP addresses and other records.

course.learn: DNS attacks manipulate or abuse name-resolution infrastructure. Techniques can redirect users, poison cached records, tunnel data, or overwhelm DNS services.
course.why: Users depend on DNS to find legitimate services; corrupt resolution can silently send them elsewhere.
course.example: A poisoned DNS cache resolves a bank's domain to an attacker-controlled IP address.
course.exam: Unexpected DNS responses, unusual query volume, odd domains, or changed records can indicate DNS abuse.

course.exam: Look for unexpected SSIDs/APs, repeated disconnects, signal anomalies, and clients joining an unauthorized AP.

defs: An attacker secretly intercepts traffic between parties and may observe or alter communications.

course.learn: An on-path attack places the attacker between communicating parties so traffic can be observed, redirected, or altered without either endpoint realizing it.
course.why: Unprotected traffic can reveal credentials or allow session manipulation.
course.example: A malicious Wi-Fi hotspot intercepts a victim's unencrypted HTTP session and changes responses in transit.
course.exam: Certificate warnings, ARP anomalies, unexpected gateways, or changed traffic can be clues. Strong authenticated encryption helps prevent useful interception.

course.learn: Credential replay uses previously captured authentication material—such as a token, hash, ticket, or session value—to impersonate a user without knowing the original secret.
course.why: If authentication data can be reused, stealing it may be enough to bypass normal login checks.
course.example: An attacker steals a session token from a browser and reuses it from another machine to access the account.
course.exam: Replay = reuse captured proof. Nonces, timestamps, short-lived tokens, channel binding, and challenge-response help prevent reuse.

slides.teach: Learn the attacker behavior, the evidence it leaves behind, and the control that best detects or mitigates it.

course.learn: Malicious-code attacks involve unauthorized code executing on a system to steal data, alter behavior, persist, or disrupt operations.
course.why: Code execution often becomes the bridge from initial access to broader compromise.
course.example: A user opens a malicious document that launches a script and installs a backdoor.
course.exam: Unexpected processes, scripts, persistence entries, file changes, and outbound connections are common indicators.
